events.event: Green Mill opens as Pop Morse's Roadhouse, 4802 N. Broadway (Uptown)
Sutherland Hotel building completed as General Hospital #32 (military hospital); decommissioned May 1919
building purchased, rehabilitated, and named the Sutherland (for William J. Sutherland)
Regal Theater opens, 4719 South Parkway, Bronzeville
Grand Terrace Cafe opens, 3955 South Parkway Blvd
Savoy Ballroom era as jazz center begins (1928–1948 per UChicago exhibit)
National Theater Corporation sells Regal to Balaban & Katz
Club DeLisa opens, 5521 S. State St.
Ken Blewett becomes Regal manager (first Black B&K house manager; to 1959)
original Club DeLisa building burns; New Club DeLisa built nearby
Rhumboogie Café opens, 343 E. 55th St., owned by Charlie Glenn and Joe Louis
T-Bone Walker first performs at Rhumboogie (Milt Larkin band residency)
Rhumboogie Recording Company records T-Bone Walker (house band led by Marl Young); distributed by Mercury
fire closes Rhumboogie Café
Rhumboogie reopens
Rhumboogie closes for good
Theresa's Lounge opens, 4801 S. Indiana Ave. basement, by Theresa Needham
Sutherland Hotel integrated under new ownership; Black manager Earl Clark Ormes
Herman Roberts opens the Lucky Spot; Kitty Kat opens on 63rd St.
Roberts Show Club opens in converted taxicab garage; live music begins at Theresa's (singer Carl Jones brings band)
Savoy Ballroom era ends (per UChicago exhibit 1928–1948; Lindström map says 1927–1954)
Sutherland Lounge advertised as "Where the Stars and Celebrities Meet"; Sun Ra plays Roberts Show Club (June 24)
Club DeLisa closes
Ray Charles at Roberts Show Club (w/ Redd Foxx)
Roberts opens first Roberts Motel
John Coltrane Quintet recorded live at Sutherland Hotel Lounge (dates disputed: Mar 1 vs. Oct 10–15)
Stevie Wonder's "Fingertips" recorded live at Regal (Motortown Revue)
Sutherland Lounge closes "for repairs"
Miles Davis at Sutherland Lounge
Sutherland Lounge closes again after brief reopening; jazz era ends
B.B. King records "Live at the Regal"
Club DeLisa building reopens as "The Club"
Regal closes; Kingston Mines (theatre/café) opens
Kingston Mines Café acquired by Doc Pellegrino; Checkerboard Lounge founded by L.C. Thurman & Buddy Guy, 423 E. 43rd St.
Regal Theater demolished
The Warehouse opens at 206 S. Jefferson St.; Frankie Knuckles resident DJ
B.L.U.E.S. opens, 2519 N. Halsted
Muddy Waters + Jagger/Richards/Wood at Checkerboard Lounge
The Warehouse closes; Ron Hardy era begins at rebranded Muzic Box; Kingston Mines moves to 2548 N. Halsted; Sutherland Hotel closes
Frankie Knuckles opens the Power Plant, 1015 N. Halsted; Lee's Unleaded Blues opens (7401 S. South Chicago Ave.); Muzic Box runs 1983–1988
Theresa's leaves 4801 S. Indiana; closes for good a few years later
Buddy Guy leaves Checkerboard; Green Mill poetry slam launches (first Uptown Poetry Slam July 25, 1986)
Knuckles leaves Power Plant for NYC (Def Mix); Dave Jemilo-era Green Mill restoration per lore
B.L.U.E.S. Etcetera operates at 1122/1124 W. Belmont
Sutherland Hotel converted to affordable housing
Avalon Theater renamed New Regal Theater (per architecture.org "late 1980s"; Chicago Landmark designation 1992-06-17); Theresa Needham dies
Gerri's Palm Tavern shut down by the city; Stan Davis buys Lee's Unleaded Blues
Checkerboard closes (April, code violations), moves to 5201 S. Harper Court, Hyde Park (reopens Nov)
Jefferson St. block renamed "Frankie Knuckles Way" (Frankie Knuckles Day)
Sutherland Hotel listed on National Register of Historic Places
"Live at the Checkerboard Lounge, Chicago 1981" released
Checkerboard closes after L.C. Thurman's death; Lee's Unleaded Blues closes
Berger acquires Lee's building; Doc Pellegrino dies (Kingston Mines to daughters Donna & Lisa)
Kingston Mines and B.L.U.E.S. close (pandemic)
Warehouse building sold to two lawyers; listed for redevelopment
The Warehouse designated a Chicago Landmark
Lee's Unleaded Blues reopens
Brunswick label founded by Brunswick-Balke-Collender piano makers
Leonard Chess buys a stake in Aristocrat Records
Chess Records founded in Chicago by Leonard and Phil Chess (renamed from Aristocrat); Chance Records founded in Chicago by Art Sheridan
Checker Records started as Chess subsidiary; Parrot Records founded in Chicago by DJ Al Benson

Vee-Jay Records founded in Gary, Indiana, by Vivian Carter and James C. Bracken; Arc Music (BMI) publishing set up by Leonard Chess and Gene Goodman; Delmar Records founded in St. Louis by Bob Koester
Chance Records closes (end of year); Art Sheridan becomes a Vee-Jay financial backer; Vee-Jay's earliest recordings cut at Chance's Chicago studio
Vee-Jay buys downtown Chicago offices at 2129 S. Michigan Avenue ("Record Row"); the El Dorados give Vee-Jay its first national pop-chart hit
Ewart Abner leaves Chance to join Vee-Jay as general manager (Wikipedia: 1955; Smithsonian: 1954
events.source: disputed); Chess launches jazz/pop label Marterry, quickly renamed Argo — Wikipedia (Vee-Jay Records); Wikipedia (Argo Records) [Disputed on Abner year; Verified on Argo]

events.event: Cobra Records begins operating (through 1959); Chess moves to 2120 S. Michigan Avenue (May 1957 per Chicago landmark publication
events.source: the commonly cited move year is 1957; one source says 1956) — alchetron.com; Wikipedia (Chess Records) [Provisional/Disputed on exact month-year of move]

events.event: Brunswick's R&B era begins with Jackie Wilson's "Reet Petite"; Nat Tarnopol joins as A&R head
Koester moves Delmark to Chicago; Vee-Jay starts its jazz line under Sid McCoy; Jerry Butler & the Impressions' "For Your Precious Love" crosses over
Curtom Publishing formed by Curtis Mayfield and Eddie Thomas (Jerry Butler silent partner)
Gene Chandler's "Duke of Earl" released on Vee-Jay; tops pop and R&B charts
Vee-Jay moves offices to Los Angeles (label leadership shakeup); Beatles licensing via EMI
Vee-Jay sells ~2.6 million Beatles singles in one month (Vee-Jay + Tollie)
Argo renamed Cadet Records; the Brackens buy Vee-Jay back and return it to Chicago, resources exhausted
Jackie Wilson comeback "Whispers" produced by Carl Davis; Davis becomes Brunswick VP of A&R with a new Michigan Avenue studio; Vee-Jay files for bankruptcy (May vs August
events.source: disputed), ~$3M in debt — Wikipedia (Nat Tarnopol); Wikipedia (Vee-Jay Records); NPR/WCMU

events.event: Vee-Jay assets bought by Betty Chiappetta and Randy Wood, renamed Vee-Jay International; Twinight Records founded in Chicago by Howard Bedno and Peter Wright (later + E. Rodney Jones); Chess relocates to 320 E. 21st Street
events.source: Wikipedia (Vee-Jay Records); Wikipedia (Twinight Records); Wikipedia (Chess Records)

events.event: Curtom Records founded in Chicago by Curtis Mayfield and Eddie Thomas
Dakar Records founded by Carl Davis; Chess brothers sell to GRT for $6.5M (early 1969); Leonard Chess dies of a heart attack, age 52 (October); Syl Johnson's "Is It Because I'm Black" on Twinight
Checker discontinued after GRT consolidation; Cadet artists moved to Chess
Dakar moves under Brunswick distribution (January); GRT folds Chess into Janus; "My Ding-A-Ling" becomes Chess's only No. 1 pop record
Cadet stops releasing records
GRT sells Chess remains to All Platinum Records
Dakar folds; Carl Davis founds Chi-Sound Records
Chi-Sound's Gene Chandler "Get Down" is a major hit
Curtom defunct
Chi-Sound's 20th Century Records distribution deal ends
Brunswick stops producing new product (150+ Billboard-charted singles)
MCA acquires rights to the Chess catalog
Chameleon Music Group's Daniel Pritzker buys VJ International from Chiapetta; 2120 S. Michigan designated a Chicago Landmark (May 16)
events.source: groovespin.com; Wikipedia (Chess Records) [Provisional on Chameleon; Verified on landmark]

events.event: Marie Dixon (Willie Dixon's widow) purchases 2120 S. Michigan
Brunswick revived by Paul and Mara Tarnopol
Blues Heaven Foundation museum opens at 2120 S. Michigan
Vee-Jay catalog licensing deal with Rhino Records (Michele Tayler)
Carl Davis dies (August 9), age 77
Phil Chess dies (October 19), age 95
Delmark sold by Koester; becomes Delmark Records LLC
Bob Koester dies (May 12), age 88
Gordon McLendon buys the station that becomes WYNR (1390 AM), drops foreign-language programming for an all-Black format; announcers include Yvonne Daniels
WVON launches on 1450 AM (ex-WHFC, Cicero), bought by Leonard and Phil Chess; "The Voice of the Negro"; original Good Guys on air
Leonard Chess dies; WVON sold to Globetrotter Communications (George Gillette, Potter Palmer)
Yvonne Daniels becomes the first female air personality at WLS
102.7 FM takes WBMX call letters ("Black Music EXperience"), urban contemporary format
Globetrotter buys WNUS AM-FM for $3,550,000; WVON moves 1450→1390; 107.5 FM becomes WGCI with a disco format ("Studio 107")
The Warehouse opens at 206 S. Jefferson (Robert Williams); Frankie Knuckles begins residency
Combined Communications buys Globetrotter (merges with Gannett 1978)
Disco Demolition Night at Comiskey Park (rock DJ Steve Dahl's promotion turns a double-header into a riot)
WXOL premieres on 1450 AM (Midway Broadcasting: Wesley South + Pervis Spann)
WGCI shifts from disco to urban contemporary
Lee Michaels assembles the Hot Mix 5 on WBMX ("Saturday Night Live, Ain't No Jive")
The Warehouse closes (period of significance ends); Knuckles departs; "Your Love" tapes begin circulating among Chicago DJs
Music Box opens with Ron Hardy as resident DJ; AM 1390 flips call letters to WGCI; Knuckles opens the Power Plant
AM 1390 call-sign change to WGCI
Jesse Saunders & Vince Lawrence release "On and On" (Jes Say); Trax Records founded (late 1984, Sherman/Saunders, Lawrence's design/signings); Scott Silz leaves Hot Mix 5, replaced by Julian Perez
events.source: RA; GO BANG!; Hot Mix 5 history

events.event: DJ International Records founded (Rocky Jones, Benji Espinoza); debut "Music Is the Key" (J.M. Silk/Steve "Silk" Hurley)
Jamie Principle's "Your Love" released on Persona Records
Marshall Jefferson's "Move Your Body" released (label attribution disputed: Trax vs. DJ International)

Mr. Fingers (Larry Heard) "Can You Feel It" on Trax; "The House Sound of Chicago" comp on DJ International; Farley "Jackmaster" Funk's "Love Can't Turn Around"; WVON flips to Black talk format; three Hot Mix 5 members defect to WGCI's "Jackmasters" (July)
events.source: multiple sources [Verified, except defect story: Provisional]

events.event: Phuture's "Acid Tracks" on Trax; Music Box closes (after-hours ordinance); first DJ International UK/European house tour (March); Knuckles's "Your Love" version on Trax
WGCI cancels the "Jackmasters" program
Fingers Inc. *Another Side* (first long-form house LP, per biographies); WBMX sold ($27M); 1988-10-18: 102.7 FM becomes WVAZ "V103" (urban AC)
AM 1390 debuts African-American talk format (WGCI-FM stays urban contemporary)
Disputed death year for Ron Hardy in some sources (Wikipedia: March 2, 1992) —
Ron Hardy dies (AIDS-related), per Wikipedia —
Knuckles wins the first Grammy for Remixer of the Year, Non-Classical
"Frankie Knuckles Way" dedicated; Frankie Knuckles Day (backed by State Sen. Barack Obama)
Rachael Cain revives/takes over Trax
Frankie Knuckles dies, age 59
Herb Kent dies, age 88, hours after his final broadcast
Larry Sherman dies, age 70
The Warehouse designated a Chicago Landmark
Warehouse landmark dedication block party
"Your Love" (Principle 1986; Knuckles 1987) added to the National Recording Registry
Pilgrim building constructed as Adler & Sullivan synagogue
Thomas A. Dorsey moves to Chicago
Pilgrim Baptist Church occupies the building
First Church of Deliverance founded by Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs; Dorsey works solely in religious music from this year
Rose Records reportedly founded as Rose Radio by Aaron Rosenbloom
Dorsey becomes Pilgrim's choral director (Verified, through late 1970s); Dorsey House of Music established (Provisional); NCGCC founded per some sources
Martin-Frye Quartet organized (Verified); NCGCC founded per other sources
First Church of Deliverance begins Sunday radio broadcasts (Verified); Morris performs at Chicago World's Fair, relocates to Chicago
"Midnight Broadcast" hour-long program on WSBC
Martin-Frye Quartet becomes the Roberta Martin Singers
Rev. Cobbs privately funds printing of Kenneth Morris's "Heaven Bells"
Roberta Martin Studio of Music founded (Provisional); electric organ introduced at First Church after its building move
Martin and Morris Music Company founded by Sallie Martin and Kenneth Morris (Verified); Morris arranges/publishes "Just a Closer Walk with Thee" (Provisional); Sallie Martin Singers formed
Muddy Waters moves to Chicago; postwar electric blues takes shape
Little Walter's first released recordings on Ora Nelle (Provisional); Morris accompanies Mahalia Jackson on "Move On Up a Little Higher"
Vee-Jay founded by Vivian Carter and James Bracken (Verified); First Church televises services on WLS-TV
WGCI first airs as WFMQ (Verified); Koester moves to Chicago
Koester takes over Seymour's Jazz Mart, renames it Jazz Record Mart
Jazz Record Mart brand dates to this year
Curtom Records founded by Curtis Mayfield and Eddie Thomas
Gramaphone Records opens (Provisional); Chi-Lites' Brunswick era begins
WGCI call letters adopted
Joe Dale and Carl Borowski take ownership of Gramaphone
Paul Weisberg starts a record pool at Importes, Etc.
Dr. Wax opens in Lincoln Park
Dr. Wax Hyde Park opens
SPIN's contemporary feature on Importes, Etc.
WGCI's "Rap Down" broadcasts; Common featured in *The Source*'s "Unsigned Hype"
Twista's debut *Runnin' Off at da Mouth*; Guinness fastest-rapper listing; Common's *Can I Borrow a Dollar?* (Oct 6, Relativity)
Maxwell Street market moved for UIC expansion
Rose Records reportedly closes
Do or Die's "Po Pimp" released independently on Creator's Way, then nationally on Rap-A-Lot
Twista's *Adrenaline Rush* on Atlantic/Big Beat
Roberta Martin Singers honored with U.S. postage stamp
Pilgrim Baptist Church fire
Maxwell Street market moves again (Verified); Dr. Wax Evanston closes
Hyde Park Records opens; last Dr. Wax location closes
Jazz Record Mart closes (27 E. Illinois); Bob's Blues & Jazz Mart opens
Pilgrim sold to the National Museum of Gospel Music
James Rosenbloom obituary confirms Rose Records' 60+ year family history (Verified); Bob Koester tributes
Gramaphone co-owner Joe Dale dies (announced March 26)
